match.reason: No existing point covers choosing between equity and debt to fund a start-up; related points on establishment, growth and liability touch funding or risk but do not teach this idea.

draft.title: Financing a new business
card: A new business needs money before it earns any. The owner has to decide where that start-up money will come from.
money the owner puts in, such as personal savings. The owner keeps control and does not owe interest, but the owner's own money is at risk if the business fails.
money borrowed, such as a bank loan. It must be repaid with interest, whether or not the business is making a profit.
Many owners use a mix of both. Using more equity means less to repay. Using more debt means the owner risks less of their own savings.
draft.remember: Equity is the owner's own money and is at risk. Debt is borrowed and must be repaid with interest.

a.q: Which statement best describes debt finance for a new business?
opts: Borrowed money that must be repaid with interest
Money the owner puts in from personal savings
Money that the owner keeps and never has to repay
Money from customers paid before the business opens
a.why: Debt is borrowed money, so it must be repaid with interest. Savings put in by the owner are equity, which is the most tempting wrong option because both are ways to start a business.
a.clue: Think about who the money belongs to at first.

b.q: Priya uses her own savings to open a bakery in Orange. Six months later the bakery closes. What is the main risk of the finance she chose?
opts: She loses her own money that she put into the business
She must repay a bank loan with interest
She gives up control of the bakery to a lender
She pays interest on the money she lost
b.why: Her savings are equity, so the money she put in is at risk if the business fails. A loan with interest is debt, which she did not use, so repayment to a bank is not her risk here.
b.clue: Where did her start-up money come from?

a.best: Borrowed money that must be repaid with interest

b.best: She loses her own money that she put into the business

problems.detail: 'Using more debt means the owner risks less of their own savings' is misleading. Many small business owners are sole traders with unlimited liability, or give personal guarantees on loans. If the business fails, they must still repay the debt from their own savings and assets, so debt does not simply protect the owner's money.

check.summary: Both questions are sound and each has exactly one right answer. The card's last line wrongly suggests that borrowing protects the owner's savings, which ignores unlimited liability and personal guarantees on loans.

proposal.title: Financing a new business

money the owner puts in, such as personal savings. The owner keeps control and does not owe interest, but the owner's own money is at risk if the business fails.
